reading.body:
Ed Pagano is named on 56 AI lobbying filings, and the clients on those filings are mostly large software and cloud companies rather than AI-native firms.

The client list runs from Salesforce and OpenAI to Microsoft, Adobe, Dropbox, Amazon and SAP. That spread matters because it shows AI lobbying is not confined to the companies building frontier models. It is also being done by the incumbents selling software and cloud services that AI features get attached to. One client, Stack Infrastructure, is a data center operator, which is the one point in this data where the AI lobbying record touches physical compute directly.

The disclosed prior government positions are all Senate and executive branch roles ending between 2004 and 2014, which is what the Lobbying Disclosure Act requires filers to list for the prior twenty years. The record names two bills, S 3982 and HR 7786, both tied to filings from 2025 or later, but it does not say what either bill would do or how the lobbyist engaged with it.

What this data does not cover is large. It counts filings, not spending, not outcomes, and not positions taken. A client named on twelve filings is not necessarily more invested than one named on five, because filings vary in scope. Nothing here shows whether any bill moved, or whether the lobbying had any effect on it. The page is a record of disclosure, and disclosure is not influence.
